Activate forecasts global Consumer Internet and Media Revenues, as defined in the page’s footnote, to rise from $1.7 trillion in 2017E to $2.0 trillion in 2021E. The forecast assigns the category $302 billion in growth and a 4.1% CAGR for 2017E–2021E, compared with approximately 3% for global GDP. Among the three listed revenue segments, Cost of Internet access—including fixed broadband, wireless, and mobile Internet access—is forecast to have the largest dollar increase ($128B) and highest CAGR (5.7%).

In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study (n=2,406), Super Fans, defined as watching 10+ hours of sports content per week, were reported as 27% of fans and 61% of hours; Social Fans, defined as watching sports content only as a social activity, were reported as 10% of fans and 6% of hours. Separately, in the U.S. in 2017, 31% of sports viewers (more than five hours of sports programming per week) cited Broadcast as a cord-cutter substitution option and 21% cited Virtual Pay TV; among non-sports viewers (no sports programming on a regular basis), the respective shares were 21% and 15% (Activate study, n=1,172).

Activate forecasts that VR will not reach scaled global adoption by 2021E; the consumer adoption chart measures users as a percentage of global population over 2016–2021E and is modeled after seventh-generation gaming consoles. The page lists limited applications outside gaming, an immersive but non-social experience, and inability to move beyond a confined area as barriers to mass adoption. The page does not numerically define the threshold for “scaled” adoption.
In 2017, news readers in each of the five selected countries reported a higher perceived-trustworthiness share for News Media than for Social Media.

The U.S. eCommerce growth matrix places grocery and automotive in its “Delayed Ecommerce Adoption” area alongside products involving first-hand experience, with food freshness and used-car condition as examples. It positions categories by 2016 category share of eCommerce sales and potential shift from physical to eCommerce; these are qualitative placements, not a measured time-to-adoption.

In Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study, 34% of podcast non-listeners (n=700) selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to podcast listening. Separately, 31% of podcast listeners (n=419) selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased podcast consumption.

Podcast survey responses distinguish audience stages: among non-listeners, 34% selected “Knowing which apps to use” as a factor that would lead to listening (n=700); among listeners, 31% selected “Recommendations” as a factor that would lead to increased consumption (n=419).

Separately, the U.S. eCommerce matrix places grocery and automotive in its delayed-adoption area alongside products involving first-hand experience, while positioning categories by 2016 eCommerce sales share and potential shift from physical to eCommerce, not by a measured adoption timetable.

Together, the findings point to a decision-design tension: the relevant diagnostic differs by audience stage in podcasts and by product category in eCommerce, so a single adoption label or intervention would blur distinctions the evidence makes.

MarketLense would recommend, where these areas are in scope, assessing podcast listening and increased consumption separately and treating the eCommerce matrix as category positioning rather than timing guidance.
In the U.S. in 2017, the top 25% of users accounted for 61% of total video time spent and 34% of total consumer spend, according to Activate’s 2017 Consumer Tech & Media Research Study.
Attention and consumer spend were distributed differently across these user cohorts.
MarketLense’s recommendation: If evaluating video monetization, assess attention and spend separately rather than treating one as a proxy for the other.
